question.text: Consider the picture above. Given that $\mathbf{r}=\lambda\mathbf{p}+\mu\mathbf{q}$, find $\lambda$ and $\mu.$
question.explanation:
In $\bigtriangleup OPR$ shown above, we have

  • $OP=3|\mathbf{p}|$
  • $\overrightarrow{OP}$ has the opposite direction to $\mathbf{p}$

Hence, $\overrightarrow{OP}=-3\mathbf{p}.$

Similarly:

  • $PR=2|\mathbf{q}|$
  • $\overrightarrow{PR}$ has the opposite direction to $\mathbf{q}$

Hence, $\overrightarrow{PR}=-2\mathbf{q}.$

Additionally,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r} &= \overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{PR} \\[3pt] &= -3\mathbf{p}-2\mathbf{q}. \end{align*}

Consequently, $\mathbf{r}=\lambda\mathbf{p}+\mu\mathbf{q}=-3\mathbf{p}-2\mathbf{q}.$

Since $\mathbf{p} \nparallel \mathbf{q},$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients, we get:

  • $\lambda=-3$ and $\mu=-2$

question.text: Consider the picture above. Given that $\mathbf{c} = \lambda \mathbf{a} + 3\mathbf{b},$ find $\lambda.$
question.explanation:
To find $\lambda,$ we want to match the expression \[ \mathbf{c} = \lambda \mathbf{a} + 3\mathbf{b}. \]

We are given that one of the components is $3\mathbf{b}.$ So, we first draw the vector $3\mathbf{b}$ from the origin. Then we complete the path to the point $C.$

Let $P$ be the endpoint of the vector $3\mathbf{b}.$ Then \[ \mathbf{c} = \overrightarrow{OP} + \overrightarrow{PC}. \]

In $\bigtriangleup OPC,$ we have:

  • $PC = 3|\mathbf{a}|$

  • $\overrightarrow{PC}$ and $\mathbf{a}$ have opposite directions

Hence, $\overrightarrow{PC} = -3\mathbf{a}.$

Additionally, \begin{align*} \mathbf{c} &= \overrightarrow{OP} + \overrightarrow{PC} \\[5pt] &= 3\mathbf{b} - 3\mathbf{a}. \end{align*}

Consequently, $\mathbf{c} = \lambda \mathbf{a} + 3\mathbf{b} = -3\mathbf{a} + 3\mathbf{b}.$

Since $\mathbf{a} \nparallel \mathbf{b},$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients of $\mathbf{a},$ we get: \[ \lambda = -3 \]

example.title: Finding a Scalar Factor When Direction Reverses

question.text: Consider the picture above. Given that $\mathbf{w}=\lambda\mathbf{u}+\mu\mathbf{v}$, find $\lambda$ and $\mu.$
question.explanation:
In $\bigtriangleup OUW$ shown above, we have

  • $OU=2|\mathbf{u}|$
  • $\overrightarrow{OU}$ and $\mathbf{u}$ have the same direction

Hence, $\overrightarrow{OU}=2\mathbf{u}.$

Similarly:

  • $UW=3|\mathbf{v}|$
  • $\overrightarrow{UW}$ has the opposite direction to $\mathbf{v}$

Hence, $\overrightarrow{UW}=-3\mathbf{v}.$

Additionally,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{w} &= \overrightarrow{OU}+\overrightarrow{UW} \\[3pt] &= 2\mathbf{u}-3\mathbf{v} . \end{align*}

Consequently, $\mathbf{w}=\lambda\mathbf{u}+\mu\mathbf{v}=2\mathbf{u}-3\mathbf{v}.$

Since $\mathbf{u} \nparallel \mathbf{v},$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients, we get:

  • $\lambda=2$ and $\mu=-3$

example.title: Finding Two Scalar Factors in a Linear Combination

question.text: Consider the diagram above, where $\overrightarrow{OC}=\mathbf{c},$ $\overrightarrow{OR}=\mathbf{r},$ and $X$ divides $\overline{CR}$ in the ratio $CX:XR=6:11.$ Express $\overrightarrow{OX}$ via the vectors $\mathbf{c}$ and $\mathbf{r}.$
question.explanation:
From the diagram, we see that \[ \overrightarrow{OX} = \overrightarrow{OC}+\overrightarrow{CX}. \]

We're told that $\overrightarrow{OC} = \mathbf{c},$ so we just need to work out $\overrightarrow{CX}.$

First, from $\triangle OCR,$ we have

\begin{align*} \overrightarrow{CR}&=\overrightarrow{CO}+\overrightarrow{OR} \\[5pt] &= -\overrightarrow{OC}+\overrightarrow{OR} \\[5pt] &= -\mathbf{c}+\mathbf{r} \\[5pt] &= \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{c}. \end{align*}

Since $CX:XR=6:11,$ we have

\[ \overrightarrow{CX}=\dfrac{6}{17} \overrightarrow{CR}=\dfrac{6}{17}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{c}). \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} \overrightarrow{OX} &= \overrightarrow{OC}+\overrightarrow{CX} \\[5pt] &= \mathbf{c} + \dfrac{6}{17}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{c}) \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{\dfrac{11}{17}}\mathbf{c} + \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{\dfrac{6}{17}}\mathbf{r}. \end{align*}
